job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Grace Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up at half five out of habit, because I grew up on my parents' dairy farm in Hollin Vale. Now I share a flat near Tarnley University, where I'm doing a master's in water engineering after a civil engineering degree. My days are lectures on flood modelling and pipe networks, and I work on a project about drainage for a small town. Last summer I spent six weeks with the county water board, mostly surveying culverts and writing reports. I owe about 31,000, and my parents can't help because the farm carries its own debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds right to me. A new tool saves an hour now and then, and the work still needs people who understand the ground and the water. I'd tell my cousins that a good trade or profession is still the safest thing, as it always was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be steady but not easy. Jobs for water engineers are with the county board, a couple of consultancies and the utility, and they hire one or two graduates a year in this region. I'd still be on a debt I'm not sure how I'll repay, and I'd still want to be near home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and apply to the county board, the two consultancies and the utility, about 20 posts in all. I'd go back to the water board and ask for a summer job again, because Mr Evans, who ran my team, said they might have a vacancy. I'd also help on the farm during calving, which saves my dad hiring someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, but a bit stretched. I'm tired in the way you get from carrying two jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the work of a water engineer like, in the places you'd go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Culverts get blocked, ditches overflow, and the board has to go out and look. I measured depths, took photos and wrote them up. Fixing a culvert is honest work and you can see what you've fixed. I loved that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your family expect of you after the master's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They expect me to come home and be useful, and also to make something of myself. Those two pull in opposite directions. My mum says we'll manage, but I've seen her checking the feed bill twice.

say: I'd tell my cousins a good **trade or profession** is still the safest thing, as it always was.
I'd say the work still needs people who understand **ground and water**.
think: I'd be steady but not easy: the board and consultancies hire **one or two** graduates a year.
The **debt** is one I'm not sure how I'll repay.
do: Apply for about **20 posts** at the county board, two consultancies and the utility.
Ask Mr Evans for a **summer job** and help with calving at the farm.
feel: **Settled but stretched**, tired from carrying two jobs.
S0.quote: Fixing a culvert is honest work and you can see what you've fixed.
fieldNote: Grace's anxiety is **money and distance**: few openings and a family farm with its own debt.
The fieldwork at the water board is where she feels most herself.
She carries two jobs, study and farm help, and notices her mother checking the feed bill.

steps.text: Apply to the county water board, two consultancies and the utility
Ask Mr Evans for a summer job on his culvert team
Help on the farm during calving so my dad avoids hiring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll cope, as people always have. Some desk jobs will change, and good. Machines do the boring part. I'd say people should learn the new tools, and learn them well, and not complain. I'd say that at church or at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think the paper side of my job is the most exposed. At the board I wrote reports from the survey photos, drew the pipe plans and did the flow calculations. Software can do all that already, almost. Software can't stand in a ditch in January and decide whether to dig. I'm betting on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly, since I've only used them a little for tidying reports. I'd do it in the evenings for a few months, and I'd ask for fieldwork roles where the paper side is a smaller part. I'd also tell Mr Evans I'm willing to do inspections and on-site work, since the board will need bodies there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but not scared. It feels like a change in the weather, not a flood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of a water engineer's work would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Report writing, drawing the plans and doing the hydraulic calculations. A colleague named Priya did the models, and she said software could do two days of her work in an hour. She was joking, mostly, but I could see she was thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does that change who you'd ask for advice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my old tutor Dr Haldane and Mr Evans. They've both seen different downturns, and they'd tell me straight. I'd also ask my dad, because he's lived through drought, milk price drops and disease, and he'd tell me not to panic.

say: I'd say we'll cope as people always have, and **learn the tools well**.
I'd say machines should do the boring part.
think: The **paper side** of my job is the most exposed: reports, plans and flow calculations.
Software can't stand in a ditch in January and decide whether to **dig**.
do: Learn the **AI tools** properly in the evenings over a few months.
Ask for **fieldwork roles** and on-site inspections at the board.
feel: **Uneasy but not scared**, like a change in the weather, not a flood.
S1.quote: Software can't stand in a ditch in January and decide whether to dig. I'm betting on that.
fieldNote: Grace bets on **fieldwork** as the shelter, in keeping with her farm upbringing.
She asks mentors and her dad, who has lived through droughts and price drops.
Priya's joke about two days of work in an hour is her concrete signal.

steps.text: Take an evening course on using AI for survey reports
Ask the water board for inspection and fieldwork roles
Talk to Dr Haldane and Mr Evans about which roles last

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we must look after one another and keep calm. I'd say that the farm and the church will matter more, not less, because people will need food and a place to belong. I'd tell people to stay local and stick together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be frightened. If the thinking work goes in two years, a water engineer's planning, modelling and design go with it. I'd finish with a debt of 31,000 and the farm is still carrying its own. Dad can't help, and I'd be the one expected to help him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the university the moment a job came and go to work, whatever it was. I'd go home and work the farm in the meantime, and take any contract work at the water board, even the mud and the ditches. I'd also talk to Dad about whether the farm should sell some land, and I wouldn't pretend that's easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Fearful, with a stone in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens on the farm in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, the farm. It has a loan, a quota and a vet bill on top of that. If I can't earn, we can't pay it, and Dad would sell cows and then land. I think of him walking the fields alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think you owe your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I owe them my time and my work, not my life. They'd say the same. But I'd feel the weight of it every month when the bank letter comes.

say: I'd say we must **look after one another** and stick together, because food and belonging will matter more.
I'd tell people to stay local.
think: The thinking work of a water engineer goes in two years, and the farm still carries its own **debt**.
If I can't earn, we can't pay the **loan**, and Dad would sell cows and then land.
do: Take **any contract work** at the water board, even the mud and the ditches.
Work the **farm** with my dad and talk through selling some land.
feel: **Heavy and fearful**, with a stone in my stomach.
S2.quote: I'd leave the university the moment a job came and go to work, whatever it was.
fieldNote: Grace's fear is about the **farm's loan**, which she calls the household's real weight.
She is willing to stop her studies for any job.
She will not pretend selling land is easy.

steps.text: Take any contract or ditch work at the county water board
Work on the farm with my dad through the dairy season
Talk with Dad about selling the top field to cut the loan
Ask the church and the farm co-op about hardship help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough for most people to find a safe path. I'd say don't wait. Save, learn and keep family close. I'd say it to cousins and friends who think it's all hype, and I'd say it kindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I think I'd get a job, learn it properly and then move into the part that needs presence, like on-site inspection, flood response, and supervising contractors. Thinking AI might do the planning by 2031, but robots won't be crawling through culverts until about 2034. I'd have about three good years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job with the water board or a consultancy, and put 150 a month on the loan and 100 toward helping the farm. I'd learn the AI tools on the job, because the board will use them. I'd keep my hands in the real work, with site visits and in the field, and make myself useful to the people who do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with a lump of worry. A bit like waiting for the vet's results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the job, and I'd go home every other weekend to help. I'd also look for any government scheme for farm succession, which helps young people take on a farm's loan. I'd read the details myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set a goal of halving the loan in five years. It's a modest goal and I think it's honest.

say: I'd say five years is long enough to find a safe path, so **save and learn**.
I'd say it kindly to cousins who think it's hype.
think: I'd move into the part that needs **presence**: inspection, flood response and supervising contractors.
Robots won't crawl through culverts until about **2034**, so I'd have about three good years.
do: Take a job with the water board and put **150 a month** on the loan and 100 toward the farm.
Learn the **AI tools** on the job and go home every other weekend.
feel: **Hopeful**, with a lump of worry, like waiting for the vet's results.
S3.quote: Thinking AI might do the planning by 2031, but robots won't be crawling through culverts until about 2034.
fieldNote: Grace reads the **three-year gap** between thinking AI and robots as her window.
Her budget splits between her own loan and the farm.
She will read farm succession schemes herself.

steps.text: Take a job with the water board or a consultancy and learn the field work
Pay 150 a month on the loan and 100 toward the farm
Go home every other weekend and check farm succession schemes
Learn the board's AI reporting tools on the job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a time to be sensible. Ten years is a long runway, and I'd say don't count on a single job or a single employer. I'd tell people it's good to be curious and good to hold on to your roots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel quite settled. I'd be 34, with an established job, the loan paid off and maybe a small plot of my own. AI would change my work a lot, and I'd have had ten years to get used to it. Robots might reach the ditches by 2039, but I'd be a supervisor by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first job, learn the tools as they arrive, and pay the loan off by about 30. I'd help Dad shift the farm toward something less risky, perhaps selling direct to shops. And I'd save to marry and have a family, probably in the village. I'd want to do things the usual way, with some changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content. A little nostalgic for how things are now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would ten years change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn a skill that matters, stay curious and be a good neighbour. Our village needs people who can go away and study, then come back if they wish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the young people in your village?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't be afraid of new things, and don't be fooled by them.

say: I'd say it's a time to be **sensible**: don't count on a single job or employer.
I'd say it's good to be curious and keep your roots.
think: I'd feel settled at 34, with a job, the loan paid off and maybe a small **plot of my own**.
Robots might reach the ditches by 2039, but I'd be a **supervisor** by then.
do: Take the first job, learn the tools, and clear the loan by about **30**.
Help Dad shift the farm to **selling direct** to shops.
feel: **Content**, a little nostalgic for how things are now.
S4.quote: Our village needs people who can go away and study, then come back if they wish.
fieldNote: Grace's ten-year picture is **rooted**: a job, a cleared loan and a plot in her village.
She sees herself as a supervisor when robots reach the ditches.
Calm is justified by her family's farm shift and her own steady pay.

steps.text: Take the first water engineering job and learn each new tool as it arrives
Clear the loan by around age 30
Help Dad start selling milk and cheese direct to shops
Buy a small plot of land near Hollin Vale

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it gives no time and the farm's debt would fall on me. What would help is a quick way into work, support for family farms with loans, and a chance to pay the degree off by working rather than waiting.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm glad someone asked what I think, rather than what I should do. I'm a bit tired of being told to adapt, when some of us have a lot of weight to carry.

headlineQuote: I'm a bit tired of being told to adapt, when some of us have a lot of weight to carry.
portrait: Grace is 24, doing a **water engineering master's** after civil engineering, with 31,000 of debt and a farm family.
She helps at calving, did six weeks of culvert surveys at a water board, and trusts fieldwork over paperwork.
She is traditional, church-going and practical, and uses AI **now and then**, mostly to tidy reports.
She is anxious to uneasy in most worlds and alarmed at two years, when the farm's loan would fall on her.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which leaves no time and puts the farm's debt on her.
whatWouldHelp: She wants quick work, support for **family farms** with loans, and a way to pay the degree off by working.
